title: Functions, Arrays and Objects
description: Learn to compose small functions and transform datasets predictably. Understand function declarations, expressions and arrows; choose map, filter, reduce, find, some or every by their result; and work with objects using destructuring and spread without accidental mutation.
learningOutcomes: Explain the difference between function declarations, function expressions and arrow functions.
Distinguish parameters, arguments, return values and side effects.
Choose an array method by the shape of the result required.
Use map, filter, reduce, find, some and every correctly on datasets.
Extract, rename and default object properties with destructuring.
Create shallow copies and transform objects without confusing a copy with deep immutability.
Build small, composable data-processing functions and explain their behavior.
Explain lexical scope and closures, including why functions resolve names from where they are created.

blocks.text: 1. Why functions matter

A function packages a named or reusable operation behind an input/output contract. Instead of repeating the same steps for every order, user or price, you describe the transformation once and call it with different data. Good functions make intent visible: inputs are explicit, the result is returned, and unrelated effects are kept out when practical.

blocks.title: A function call is not the same as a printed result
blocks.text: return sends a value back to the caller. console.log displays a value for debugging or observation. Logging a value does not return it from the function.
2. Function declarations, expressions and arrow functions

A function declaration defines a named function as a statement. A function expression creates a function value inside an expression and can assign that value to a variable. An arrow function is a concise function expression introduced by =>. These forms all let you define behavior, but their syntax and details—such as initialization timing and this binding—are not identical.

steps.title: A declaration gives the function a name
steps.explanation: formatLabel receives two parameters. The return statement produces a string; the caller receives it. A declaration can be called before its line in the same scope because the function binding is initialized during scope setup.

steps.title: An expression assigns a function value
steps.explanation: The function expression is evaluated and its result is assigned to addTax. Do not call this variable before its initialization has run: the variable binding and the function value have different initialization rules from a declaration.

steps.title: An arrow can use an implicit return
steps.explanation: Because the arrow body is a single expression with no braces, that expression's value is returned automatically. With a block body using braces, you must write return when a value is needed.

steps.title: The call receives the returned values
steps.explanation: The first call returns a formatted label, the second returns 11, and the third returns 12. The console calls only display those returned values.

blocks.text: Optional deep dive: scope and lexical environments

Scope is the language rule that determines where a binding can be referenced. A Lexical Environment is part of the ECMAScript specification's model for explaining that rule: it combines an Environment Record (the bindings associated with a scope) with a link to an outer environment. Engines need not implement this model as literal objects, but it is a precise way to reason about nested functions, shadowing, and closures.

items: Lexical scope follows the nesting in source code. A function uses the surrounding lexical environment where it was created, not the local variables of the function that happens to call it.
When an inner scope cannot resolve a name locally, lookup continues through the outer-environment chain until a binding is found or the lookup reaches the outermost environment.

A function object retains access to the lexical environment from its creation. In ECMAScript this relationship is represented by an internal [[Environment]] slot; normal application code cannot inspect or edit that slot directly.
Shadowing means an inner scope declares a binding with the same name as an outer binding. References in the inner scope resolve to the nearer binding.

A closure is a function together with access to the surrounding lexical bindings it uses. It keeps those bindings reachable while the closure remains reachable; it does not freeze their values into a snapshot.

steps.title: Create a local binding that shadows the global one
steps.explanation: There are two bindings named name: the outer binding "Alex" and the local binding "John" inside start. The inner declaration shadows the outer binding within start.

steps.title: Create greet inside start's lexical environment
steps.explanation: The returned function is created while start's local name binding is in scope. The function retains access to that lexical environment after start returns.

steps.title: Call greet from a different scope
steps.explanation: callGreet has its own local name value "Sam", but greet was not declared inside callGreet. That caller-local binding is not part of greet's lexical lookup chain.

steps.title: Resolve name from where greet was created
steps.explanation: The output is "John". Variable lookup uses greet's lexical environment, not the call site and not simply the nearest name in the current call stack.

blocks.text: A closure retains access to bindings, not a frozen copy of every value. If the captured variable is reassigned or incremented, later calls to the closure can observe the updated binding. This is why closures are useful for private state, function factories, and callbacks that need to remember context across separate events.

steps.title: Create state inside a function call
steps.explanation: Each call to createCounter creates a new local count binding initialized to zero.

steps.title: Return a function that closes over the binding
steps.explanation: increment can read and update count even after createCounter has returned, because the closure keeps the needed lexical binding reachable.

steps.title: Create two independent counters
steps.explanation: first and second are closures created by separate calls, so they refer to different count bindings.

steps.title: Observe shared state within one closure and independent state across closures
steps.explanation: Calling first twice produces 1 then 2. Calling second produces 1 because its own count is still zero before that call.

blocks.prompt: A function returned from start() reads a variable declared inside start(), even after start() has returned. Why?

options.text: The returned function retains access to the lexical environment where it was created
options.feedback: A closure keeps access to the surrounding lexical bindings its function body uses.

options.text: JavaScript searches the caller's local variables before the function's outer scope
options.feedback: Lexical lookup follows the function's declaration environment, not the caller's local bindings.

options.text: return copies every local variable into a global object
options.feedback: Returning a function does not copy all locals to the global object.

options.text: The function body is re-parsed every time it is called to choose the nearest variable
options.feedback: Calling the function does not change where its lexical scope is rooted.

blocks.explanation: Function creation establishes lexical scope. A returned inner function can keep the needed outer bindings reachable after the outer call finishes.

items: Declaration: function calculateTotal(items) { ... } — useful for named operations and direct declarations.
Function expression: const calculateTotal = function (items) { ... }; — the function value is assigned when the expression runs.
Arrow expression: const double = (value) => value * 2; — compact callbacks and transformations; it does not create its own this or arguments.
Parameters are names in the function definition; arguments are the values supplied at the call site.
A return value can be assigned, passed to another function, transformed or tested. A function that reaches its end without return returns undefined.

blocks.title: Do not choose arrows just because they are shorter
blocks.text: Arrow functions inherit this from their surrounding lexical context and do not have their own arguments object. That is helpful for callbacks, but it means an arrow is not a drop-in replacement for every object method or constructor.
3. Inputs, return values and side effects

Prefer a function that receives the values it needs and returns its result. For example, a function that totals prices is easier to test if it does not secretly read a global array or update the DOM. This does not mean every useful function must be pure: UI handlers and network code necessarily interact with the outside world. The goal is to make that boundary deliberate.

items: Identify the required inputs and represent them as parameters.
Compute the result using local variables and clear steps.
Return the value when a caller needs to use it.
Keep side effects such as logging, DOM updates, network calls or storage writes explicit.
Name the function according to the operation and the shape of its result.

blocks.text: 4. Select an array method by its result

Array methods are not interchangeable loop shortcuts. Their most useful distinction is the result they produce. For an ordinary dense array, map produces one transformed output per input item; filter keeps only items whose predicate is truthy; find returns the first matching item or undefined; some and every return booleans; reduce combines the items into one accumulated result.

items: map(callback) → a new array containing each callback result.
filter(predicate) → a new array containing matching elements.
find(predicate) → the first matching element, or undefined when none matches.
some(predicate) → true when at least one element matches; otherwise false.
every(predicate) → true when every element matches; otherwise false.
reduce(reducer, initialValue) → one accumulated result such as a number, object or grouped structure.

steps.title: Start from one source array
steps.explanation: amounts is the input dataset. The following methods produce new arrays instead of replacing the original variable.

steps.title: Filter decides which elements remain
steps.explanation: The predicate amount >= 10 returns a boolean for each value. Only 12 and 20 satisfy it, so expensive contains two elements.

steps.title: Map transforms every remaining element
steps.explanation: The mapping callback converts each retained number to a formatted string. The output has the same number of elements as the filtered input.

steps.title: The arrays show different responsibilities
steps.explanation: expensive contains numbers; labels contains strings. The source amounts array remains [12, 5, 20, 8].

blocks.text: 4.1. Chaining transforms

A chain reads from left to right: the output of one method becomes the input of the next. In activeCards below, filter narrows the set before map projects each remaining object into a smaller display model. This is often clearer than mutating a shared array in several steps.

blocks.caption: Filter first, then project the fields the UI needs.

blocks.title: New array does not mean deep clone
blocks.text: map and filter create new arrays, but if their output contains objects, those objects may still be the same object references from the input. Avoid mutating nested data unless that is intentional.
4.2. Use reduce when you need an accumulated value

reduce repeatedly calls a reducer with the current accumulator and the next item. Supplying an initial value makes the intended starting state explicit and allows an empty array to be handled. Without an initial value, an empty array throws and a non-empty array uses its first element as the initial accumulator—behavior that is easy to overlook.

steps.title: Give the accumulator a clear starting value
steps.explanation: sum begins at zero, then accumulates each price: 0 + 12, then + 8, then + 5.

steps.title: The final accumulator is the result
steps.explanation: After all prices have been processed, total is 25 and reduce returns that value.

steps.title: An explicit initial value handles empty data
steps.explanation: There are no prices to add, so the reducer is never called and the initial value zero is returned.

blocks.title: A quick selection rule
blocks.text: Need one output per item? Start with map. Need fewer items? Use filter. Need the first match? Use find. Need a yes/no answer? Use some or every. Need one combined value? Use reduce.

blocks.prompt: Given const values = [2, 4, 6], what does values.map((value) => value * 10) return?

options.feedback: map calls the callback for each value and collects each returned product, so the new array contains 20, 40 and 60.
That shape suggests filtering some values; map does not remove the 2, 4 or 6 when the callback returns a value.
That is a single combined number, but map returns an array of individual callback results.
A boolean is often returned by some or every, not by this numeric mapping callback.

blocks.explanation: map transforms each input element into one corresponding output element.

blocks.prompt: Which of these methods return a boolean for the whole array based on a predicate? Select all that apply.

options.feedback: some returns true when at least one item satisfies the predicate, otherwise false.
every returns true when all items satisfy the predicate, otherwise false.
filter returns an array of matching items rather than a boolean summary.
find returns the first matching element or undefined, not a boolean.

blocks.explanation: some and every summarize a predicate over the collection with a boolean result.

options.feedback: No element satisfies value > 20, so find returns undefined.
find returns a matching element or undefined; it does not reduce the search result to a boolean.
An empty array is a possible filter result, but find returns a single element or undefined.
11 is the final value in the array, but it does not satisfy the predicate value > 20.

blocks.explanation: find stops at the first matching item. If there is no match, the result is undefined.

blocks.text: 5. Objects, destructuring and spread

Objects model related values with named properties. In real frontend code, data commonly arrives as an object from an API, gets normalized or selected, then becomes a view model for a component. Destructuring makes property access concise; spread helps create a shallow copy with selected changes. Neither feature removes the need to understand ownership and mutation.

steps.title: Extract and rename a property
steps.explanation: The property name is name, but the local binding is displayName. The role binding receives the existing value editor; its default viewer would be used only when role were undefined.

steps.title: Spread copies the top-level properties
steps.explanation: updatedUser gets the enumerable own properties from user, then role is overwritten with admin because the later property wins.

steps.title: Rest collects remaining properties
steps.explanation: The role property is extracted as currentRole. The rest pattern collects other remaining top-level properties into publicProfile.

steps.title: The values can be used independently
steps.explanation: The local binding role still contains editor. updatedUser has admin, and publicProfile contains id and name but no role property.

items: const { name } = user extracts the name property into a binding named name.
const { name: displayName } = user renames the local binding; it does not rename the source property.
const { role = "viewer" } = user uses the default only when role is undefined, not when it is null.
const [first, second] = items extracts array elements by position.
const { role, ...rest } = user collects the remaining enumerable own properties after role is removed from the pattern.

blocks.text: 5.1. Spread creates shallow copies

A copy made with object spread copies the top-level property values. When one of those values is another object or array, the nested reference is copied, not the nested object itself. That is why changing copy.preferences.theme below is visible through original.preferences.theme as well.

steps.title: Copy the first-level properties
steps.explanation: copy is a different outer object, but its preferences property points to the same nested object as original.preferences.

steps.title: Mutate a shared nested object
steps.explanation: The nested preferences object is shared, so changing its theme through copy also changes what original.preferences.theme reads.

steps.title: Copy nested state explicitly when needed
steps.explanation: Spreading preferences separately gives independentCopy a new nested preferences object. For more deeply nested data, choose an explicit update strategy rather than assuming one spread creates a deep clone.

blocks.text: 5.2. Transform API-shaped data into a view model

One common frontend task is selecting active records and shaping them into the small objects a list component needs. The pipeline below filters by active, then maps each selected object to a new object with only id and label. The original records remain available for other uses.

blocks.caption: A common filter → map data preparation pattern.

blocks.prompt: Why should a sum calculated with reduce usually provide an initial value of 0?

options.text: It defines the accumulator's starting state and makes an empty array return 0
options.feedback: The reducer starts from zero, and an empty array returns that initial accumulator without calling the callback.

options.text: It makes reduce mutate the original array
options.feedback: The initial accumulator does not cause mutation; reduce returns the accumulated result and leaves the array itself unchanged unless the callback mutates external data.

options.text: It forces each array element to be converted to a number
options.feedback: An initial value does not automatically validate or convert each item; the callback defines how values are combined.

options.text: It guarantees the reducer runs exactly once
options.feedback: For a non-empty array, the reducer is called for each element; for an empty array with an initial value, the callback is not called.

blocks.explanation: An initial value makes the accumulator contract explicit and handles empty data safely.

blocks.prompt: Which statement extracts user.name into a local variable called displayName?

options.feedback: In object destructuring, the property to read appears before the colon and the local binding appears after it.
This reads user.displayName and creates a local binding called name, which is the reverse of the requested mapping.
Square brackets are used for array destructuring, and this is not valid JavaScript destructuring syntax.
A colon cannot be used in this position to access an object property; dot access would be user.name.

blocks.explanation: The syntax { property: localName } reads the named property and binds its value under a different local name.

blocks.prompt: After const copy = { ...original }, what is generally true when original.preferences is itself an object?

options.text: copy is a new outer object, but copy.preferences can reference the same nested object
options.feedback: Object spread copies top-level property values. A nested object value is copied as a reference, not recursively cloned.

options.text: Both the outer object and every nested object are guaranteed to be deep-cloned
options.feedback: Spread performs a shallow copy; it does not recursively clone nested arrays or objects.

options.text: original and copy become the same outer object
options.feedback: The spread expression creates a new outer object, although some property values may still be shared.

options.text: All properties from original are omitted unless they are primitives
options.feedback: Enumerable own properties are copied regardless of whether their values are primitive or objects.

blocks.explanation: Shallow copy creates a new outer object but preserves references held by nested object-valued properties.

Use the named array methods where requested rather than replacing every operation with a loop.

blocks.text: Deep dive: closures, object identity, and immutable updates

A closure retains access to the lexical environment where a function was created, even after the outer call returns. Each factory call can create a different private binding. Separately, assigning an object to another variable copies its reference, not a recursively independent value. Spread creates a shallow copy; nested references can remain shared. These facts explain state leaks and mutation bugs in frontend code.

steps.title: The returned function closes over a binding
steps.explanation: The inner function keeps access to the count binding from this call to makeCounter. That binding remains reachable while the returned function can use it.

steps.title: Separate factory calls mean separate counters
steps.explanation: first and second close over bindings created by different calls. Reusing the same function factory does not mean its internal state is shared.

steps.title: Spread only copies the outer object
steps.explanation: copy and source are different outer objects, but both profile properties point to the same nested object. Mutating its city is visible through both references.

blocks.title: For nested state, copy every changed level
blocks.text: If you update `{ profile: { city } }`, copying only the outer object is insufficient. Create a new profile object too. In React, mutating an existing state object and passing the same reference back makes change detection and debugging unreliable.

blocks.prompt: Why does changing `copy.profile.city` also change what `source.profile.city` reads?

options.feedback: Object spread copies own enumerable properties one level deep; nested object references are preserved.

options.text: Both outer objects still reference the same nested profile object
options.feedback: The top-level objects are different, but their profile properties point at the same object, so the mutation is visible through both.

options.text: A closure merges all objects created in one file
options.feedback: Closures preserve access to lexical bindings; they do not merge objects.
Ordinary JavaScript objects are mutable unless you impose a separate restriction.

blocks.explanation: Object identity and shallow copying matter when you update arrays and nested data.

blocks.context: Practice closure reasoning and safe updates to nested objects, both common in interviews and React state code.

Two counter instances keep independent values.
updateCity returns new outer-user and profile references.
The original argument still has its original city.

Call makeCounter twice to test independence rather than only calling one counter repeatedly.

items: A closure keeps access to lexical bindings from the function's creation environment.
Each stateful factory call can create independent private state.
Spread is shallow; copy nested objects explicitly when changing nested data.

blocks.text: 5.2. Array destructuring and rest

An array pattern reads values in order from an iterable; a comma skips a position, a default applies only when the value is undefined, and a rest binding creates a new array from the remaining values and must come last. This is not name-based lookup as in an object pattern.

steps.title: Match positions
steps.explanation: first receives position 0; the empty slot skips position 1. third reads position 2.

steps.title: Apply the default and rest
steps.explanation: Position 2 is undefined, so third becomes 99. rest collects the remaining [40, 50]. If the value were null, the default would not run.

steps.title: Check the values
steps.explanation: The output is 10, then 99, then [40, 50]. A missing position in a shorter iterable becomes undefined.

blocks.prompt: What is assigned to first by `const [first = "fallback"] = [null]`?

options.text: "fallback", because null means the value is missing.
options.feedback: null is an explicit value; a destructuring default runs only for undefined.
Correct. To replace null too, apply nullish coalescing after extraction.
The array contains null at this position, so null is assigned to first.

options.text: A TypeError because arrays cannot be destructured.
options.feedback: An array is iterable and can be used with array destructuring.

blocks.explanation: A destructuring default triggers only for undefined; null, 0, false, and an empty string are preserved.

blocks.text: Rest gathers arguments; spread passes elements

steps.title: Gather the remaining arguments
steps.explanation: The rest parameter gathers every argument after label into the amounts array; it must be the final parameter.

steps.title: Expand an iterable at the call site
steps.explanation: Spread passes 4 and 6 separately. The function receives them just like total("points", 4, 6) and prints points: 10.

blocks.title: Same `...`, opposite direction
blocks.text: In parameters or destructuring, rest gathers values; in a function call or literal, spread expands an iterable/properties. Spread copies an array/object shallowly: nested references remain shared.
Optional chaining and nullish coalescing

steps.title: Guard a chain against nullish values
steps.explanation: ?. stops access when the previous part is null/undefined. The chain returns the empty nickname because user and profile exist.

steps.title: Choose a fallback rule intentionally
steps.explanation: ?? replaces only null/undefined, so score remains 0. || replaces any falsy value, so legacyScore becomes 10.

steps.title: Compare the result
steps.explanation: The output is an empty string, 0, and 10. Do not use || as a universal default when 0, false, or an empty string is valid.

blocks.title: Optional chaining does not fix every data error
blocks.text: If a variable was never declared, `unknownUser?.name` still throws ReferenceError. And `response?.user.name` guards response but not a null user; add ?. at each potentially nullish link deliberately and validate external data.

blocks.prompt: What does `const count = 0; count ?? 5` return, and how does it differ from `count || 5`?

options.feedback: || treats 0 as falsy, but ?? replaces only null and undefined.
Correct. The right choice depends on whether 0 is a real value or means absent.
The operators behave the other way around: ?? preserves 0.
Both operators are valid JavaScript; mixing ?? directly with &&/|| requires parentheses.

blocks.explanation: Nullish coalescing is for null/undefined, while logical OR uses the full falsy set. They cannot be mixed directly with &&/|| without explicit parentheses.

items: Array destructuring consumes an iterable by position; holes skip, defaults replace only undefined, and rest collects the remainder.
Rest gathers values at a binding/parameter site; spread expands them at a call or literal site.
Optional chaining short-circuits null/undefined access; nullish coalescing preserves valid falsy values such as 0 and ''.
Treat external data as untrusted and choose fallback semantics deliberately.

blocks.text: 6. Summary and interview-ready explanations

items: Declarations, expressions and arrows all define functions, but they have different syntax and initialization behavior.
Return a result to the caller; logging is an observable side effect and is not a substitute for return.
Use map for transformation, filter for selection, find for the first match, some/every for boolean predicates, and reduce for accumulation.
Supply a reduce initial value when the empty-input behavior should be predictable.
Destructuring reads properties or positions into bindings; the colon in object patterns can rename a binding.
Spread copies only one level. Nested object references can remain shared.
Prefer small transformations whose names, inputs, outputs and side effects are easy to explain.
